headings: 4.1a What is Force, and What Does It Do?
4.1b Newton's First Law — the Law of Laziness (Inertia)
4.1d Newton's Third Law — Action and Reaction
4.3 Mass and Weight — Not the Same Thing!

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you saw Raja lurch forward when the bus braked. Below are the official physics laws (Newton's 3 Laws), formulas (F = ma), and textbook calculations explaining why!

When you kick a ball, push a door, or lift a bag — do you know what you're actually doing? You're applying a force ! A push or a pull, in the simplest sense, is a force. You can't see a force directly, but you can always see what it does.

A force acting on an object can do four things: (1) start a body that is at rest, (2) stop a body that is moving, (3) change the speed of a moving body (speed it up or slow it down), or (4) change its direction (like a cricket ball changing direction when hit by a bat). Sometimes a force also changes an object's shape — squeeze a rubber ball, and it deforms.

But just applying a force doesn't always mean an object starts moving! Try pushing gently on a heavy table — it won't budge. Why? Because friction from the floor pushes back against you with an equal opposing force. As long as the force you apply and the opposing friction force are balanced , they cancel out — no motion starts. Only when your force grows bigger than friction does the table finally move. What decides "does it move or not" is whether there's an unbalanced force acting.

Here's a secret — every object has a bit of "laziness" built into it! Something at rest wants to stay at rest, and something moving wants to keep moving at the same speed and direction, until a force comes along and makes it change. This "resistance to change" is called inertia .

Want to see it directly? Think of a carrom board game. The powder sprinkled on it reduces friction. Flick the striker with your finger, and it slides a long way — because there's almost no friction force trying to stop it. That "keeps going" tendency is inertia. Same reason you lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly — your body "wants" to keep moving even though the bus has stopped!
The bus is moving forward at speed.
It brakes suddenly — the bus stops.
But your body still "wants" the forward speed — so you tip forward.
The bus is at rest, and so are you.
It suddenly starts moving forward.
Your body still "wants" to stay at rest — so you feel pushed backward.

This is exactly why wearing a seatbelt matters — in a crash, the car stops suddenly, but your body still "wants" to keep moving forward (inertia!). Without a seatbelt, you'd fly forward into the steering wheel or windscreen. The seatbelt holds you safely and controls that forward motion.
The first law tells us when motion starts or changes. The second law tells us how much it changes — specifically, how much acceleration results from applying a force.

Think of two things: (1) For the same mass, a bigger force gives a bigger acceleration — so acceleration is directly proportional to force (a ∝ F). (2) For the same force, a heavier object accelerates less — so acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (a ∝ 1/m). A perfect everyday example — pushing an empty cart is easy, but the same cart loaded with heavy goods is hard to push — more mass means less acceleration for the same push.

Combine the two: a ∝ F/m. Add a constant of proportionality, so F/m ÷ a = a constant. The unit of force is defined so that this constant becomes exactly 1 — that is, the force needed to give a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 ms⁻² is defined as one newton (N). That makes F/m ÷ a = 1, i.e. F = ma — this small, powerful equation is Newton's Second Law!

This one equation can be used three ways — whichever value is unknown, find it from the other two: Need F? F = ma. Need a? a = F/m. Need m? m = F/a. We'll work through all three in the Examples section below.

This means — when you push something, it pushes you back, equally and in the opposite direction! Hard to believe? Think of a balloon — when you let go of an inflated balloon, air rushes out one way (the action), so the balloon shoots off the other way (the reaction)! The same principle sends rockets into space.

More examples — a rower pushes the water backward with the oar (the action), and the water pushes the boat forward (the reaction) — so the boat moves forward. Swimmers push water backward with their hands, and the water pushes them forward. If two kids on skateboards push against each other, both get pushed apart in opposite directions!
Action and reaction always act on two different objects — never on the same one! The rower acts on the water; the water reacts on the boat.
That's why they don't cancel out and leave everything motionless — since they act on different objects, each produces its own separate effect.

Picture two balls moving at the same speed — a small table-tennis ball and a heavy bowling ball. Both move at the same speed, but which one is harder to stop? The heavy one — because it has more mass. Now roll the same ball at two different speeds — the faster one is harder to stop. So what decides "how hard it is to stop" is mass and velocity together. This combination is called momentum .

A fast-moving motor vehicle has a lot of momentum — that's exactly why it needs a longer distance and more time to stop. As speed decreases gradually, momentum decreases; as speed increases, momentum increases too.

Newton's Second Law can be stated even more generally as: force is the rate of change of momentum (F = Δp / Δt). For a constant mass, this works out to exactly F = ma. You can see this live in the Force Lab below!
Every day we say "weight" — but scientifically there are two separate ideas hiding in that word: mass and weight . Mixing these up is one of the most common mistakes — read carefully!
The amount of matter contained in an object.
Stays the same no matter where you are (Earth, Moon, space) — never changes.
The gravitational force pulling an object toward the centre of the Earth (or any planet).
Unit: N (newton) — it's a force!
Changes from place to place — as gravity changes, weight changes.
It's a vector quantity — always directed downward.

Applying Newton's Second Law (F = ma) to weight, using the gravitational acceleration (g): Weight (W) = mass (m) × gravitational acceleration (g) . On Earth, g ≈ 10 ms -2 (for easy calculation) — so a 1 kg mass has a weight of 10 N.

This leads to something amazing — take a 3 kg object to the Moon, and its mass is still 3 kg (the matter hasn't changed). But since gravity on the Moon is only 1/6 of Earth's, its weight there is only 1/6 of what it was on Earth . That's exactly why astronauts can jump so easily on the Moon — their mass didn't change, but their weight did!
Mass ≠ Weight. Everyday speech saying "weight is 60 kg" is technically wrong (kg is the unit of mass) — correctly: "mass is 60 kg," "weight is 600 N." Don't mix up the units (kg vs N) in an exam.
All three values in F = ma need the right units — mass always in kg (divide by 1000 if given in grams!), acceleration in ms -2 , and force comes out in N.
Action and reaction never cancel on one object. They act on two different objects — don't wrongly assume "two opposite forces on the same object" and conclude "so it won't move."

Momentum is a vector quantity — because velocity has direction, momentum does too. If direction reverses, the sign of momentum reverses too (e.g. momentum going up is positive, coming down is negative).

headings: 5.1 What is Friction, and Where Does It Come From?
5.3 What Affects Limiting Friction — and What Doesn't
5.4 Friction in Daily Life — Reducing It, and Using It

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you saw surfaces resisting motion. Below are the official laws of friction, limiting friction formulas, and practical calculations!

Roll a ball along the ground — it travels a bit, slows down gradually, and finally stops, right? We have all seen an object moving over a rough surface lose speed little by little and come to rest. The reason: the rough surface opposes the object's motion!

Try pushing a heavy bookshelf across the floor — it's tough, right? That difficulty has a name: friction . When two surfaces are in contact and one tries to slide (or actually slides) over the other, a force arises from those surfaces that opposes that sliding motion — that's the friction force.

Here's the secret — no matter how "smooth" something looks, no surface is 100% perfectly flat. At the microscopic level, every surface has tiny bumps and dips invisible to the eye. Put two surfaces together, and these tiny bumps catch on each other, resisting the slide — that's exactly where friction comes from. That's why rougher surfaces produce more friction than smoother ones.

Rub your palm slowly on a table — does it warm up? That heat is energy produced by friction! Friction always produces heat — that's exactly why the old method of rubbing two sticks together makes fire.

Take a heavy wooden block on a table, and pull it with a spring balance, little by little. Pull gently at first, and the block doesn't move — but your pulling force isn't wasted either, because friction "matches" it exactly. This is the first type.
Acts when a force is applied but the object still hasn't started moving.
A "self-adjusting" force — it grows to exactly match however much you pull, up to a limit.
The maximum static friction — right at the instant the object is just about to start moving.
Only once your force exceeds this value does the object actually start moving.
The friction that acts on an object while it is already moving, opposing that motion.
Slightly less than limiting friction — that's exactly why it's harder to start moving a heavy object than to keep it moving once it's already sliding!
The textbook investigates this with three experiments. Let's look at each.
Pulling the same block over sandpapers of different roughness, the rougher paper makes the spring balance read a higher value — meaning more force (more friction) is needed.

A simple example — moving an empty box is easy, but fill it with stones to make it heavy, and it's much harder to push — weight went up, so friction went up too. In the textbook's experiment (Activity 5.4), stacking more and more blocks (each 20 N) on top and pulling them shows the required limiting friction force steadily increasing.

Pull the same block on its long side, its short side, or its thick side — the limiting friction stays exactly the same ! It doesn't matter whether the contact area is big or small — this is something students commonly get wrong.
Friction always wastes energy (as heat) — so machines use several methods to reduce it.
Polishing/smoothing the surface — reduces roughness.
Using lubricants (oil, grease) — creates a slippery layer between the surfaces.
Using ball or roller bearings — rolling friction is much less than sliding friction. Used in bicycle wheel axles and to move heavy wood in carpentry.
Walking — the tread pattern on shoe soles increases friction and stops us from slipping.
Vehicle tyres — give grip on the road; the tread grooves channel rainwater away.
Twisting a rope — the friction between fibres (jute or nylon) is what holds the rope together. It's also why knots hold.
Brakes — a bicycle's rubber pad pressing on the rim, or a car's disc brake pads pressed on the disc by a piston — both use friction's resistance to stop the vehicle.
Surface area does not affect friction! Whether the object rests on its large face or small face, limiting friction stays the same. Don't wrongly assume "bigger area = more friction."
Static friction is not always at its maximum. It matches whatever force you apply exactly — it only increases up to the limiting friction value.
Kinetic (dynamic) friction is slightly less than limiting friction. That's why a heavy object is hardest to start moving, but slightly easier to keep sliding once it has started.

Friction is not always harmful. Walking, gripping, and braking are all impossible without it — don't treat it as something to be "eliminated entirely"; it should be reduced or increased depending on the situation.

headings: 9.1 Several Forces At Once — Which One "Wins"?
9.2 Resultant of Two Forces on the Same Line

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you observed forces pushing together and against each other. Below are the formulas and vector rules for calculating resultant forces!

A car has stalled on the road, and one person pushes — but that one person's force isn't enough to move the heavy car. A second person joins in — still not enough. Finally a third person joins, and the car starts moving! What does this tell us? When more than one force acts on the same object, they all combine to act like a single force — this single, equivalent force is called the resultant force .

This idea matters a lot — in real life, an object almost never has just one force on it (gravity, friction from the ground, and any force you apply could all act at once). To predict what the object will do, you first add up all those forces into one resultant force — this resultant is what actually decides the motion (remember Newton's laws — it's the unbalanced force that changes motion!).

Think of fishermen pulling in a fishing net — everyone pulls the same rope in the same direction. This makes it easy to haul in the net together. That's because when everyone's force is in the same direction , the resultant is simply the sum of all their forces.

But in a tug-of-war, two teams pull in opposite directions — the forces are in opposite directions . Now the resultant isn't a sum, it's a difference — the difference between the two forces, in the direction of whichever team pulled harder.
Pick one direction as positive (+) and the opposite as negative (−). Then just add all the forces up — the sign (+/−) automatically gives you the correct direction!

A single person pushes a stalled car with 150 N — it doesn't move, that force isn't enough to overcome the car's friction and weight. A second person helps by pushing in the same direction with 200 N — together they now apply 350 N — and now it moves!

The textbook demonstrates this directly with a simple experiment — spring balances at three points on a wooden strip attached to a trolley, showing that a third upward-pulling force equals the sum of two downward-pulling forces at the other points — proving that the resultant of parallel forces equals their sum.

Everything we've seen so far was forces along the same direction or line. But what happens when two forces hit an object at different angles (inclined to each other)? For example, if forces P and Q act on an object at an angle, the object won't move in P's direction, and won't move in Q's direction either — it will move in a new direction somewhere between the two !

You'll study this idea more deeply, with proper angle calculations (the parallelogram of forces), in higher grades. For now, just remember: "when directions differ, the resultant direction lies somewhere between them."
Never forget direction! First check if the forces are in the same direction or opposite. If opposite, you must subtract, not add — otherwise the answer is wrong.
The resultant always points in the direction of the LARGER force (in the opposite-direction case). Don't accidentally state the direction of the smaller force.
"Parallel" doesn't mean "same line"! Parallel forces point the same way, but they can act at different points on the object — the addition rule still applies the same.
The resultant's unit is always N (newton) — whether you add or subtract, the unit of force never changes.

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you saw forces turning a lever and see-saw. Below are the moment equations (M = F × d) and textbook equilibrium calculations!

So far we've seen force push, pull, and lift an object. But force has another job — it can also turn (rotate) an object! A door is a great example — push near the hinge and it's really hard to open, but push near the handle and it opens easily.

This turning tendency is called the moment of a force . It's what decides whether an object turns/rotates about a particular point or axis. Notice what point the door turns about? Its hinge — that point is called the turning axis (pivot) .

Measure the force needed to open a door at various points (at different distances from the hinge) with a spring balance — the farther from the hinge you push, the less force you need. But here's a surprising fact — multiply that force by the distance, and the answer is almost always the same value !
This is exactly why a longer spanner loosens a nut more easily — holding it farther from the nut (the turning axis) gives you a bigger moment for the same effort.

Hang a rod at its centre, with weights hanging on both sides — when does it stay perfectly balanced? One side going up or down happens because of a moment — so for balance, the moments on both sides must be exactly equal.

Split them into "clockwise" moments on one side and "anticlockwise" moments on the other: for balance, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment . This is exactly why, on a real see-saw, the heavier kid has to sit closer to the middle and the lighter kid has to sit at the far end!
When you turn a water tap, how do you do it? You push one finger "up" and another "down" — equal forces, opposite directions, not along the same line. This is called a couple .

Using a couple makes turning something much easier — because the two forces are opposite, they don't move the object anywhere (no net force at all), they only turn it. That's why turning a steering wheel with two hands, or a screwdriver with your fingers, feels so light.

"Distance" always means perpendicular distance! If a force acts at an angle, don't use the plain distance — use the distance measured at a right angle (90°) from the axis to the force's line of action.

Don't forget clockwise vs anticlockwise. In balance problems, add up moments on one side and set them equal to the other side — don't wrongly lump everything together as if it's all the same direction.
A couple has no net force, but it DOES have a net moment. Because the two forces are equal and opposite, they don't push/pull the object anywhere — but they still turn it.
The unit of moment is N m — not N! Force alone is in N, but the moment of a force is always in N m (newton-metre).

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you explored balancing objects. Below are the rigorous physics principles of translational and rotational equilibrium!

You've watched a tug of war. Both teams pull the rope their own way. If one side pulls harder, the rope moves that way. But if both sides pull with equal force? The rope stays perfectly still! That's because the forces on both sides are balanced — in equilibrium . We say the rope is in equilibrium.

Another example — hang a ball from a strong thread. The ball's weight pulls it down; the thread pulls it up at the same time. Since these two forces are equal, the ball just hangs there — it neither falls nor rises.

In real life an object is rarely acted on by just one force. Two, three or more forces may act — and if they balance, the object stays at rest (or keeps moving at a steady speed). In this chapter we'll look at two-force and three-force equilibrium separately. (Remember Newton's first law? With no unbalanced force, rest stays rest. This is exactly that!)

What do we need for an object under just two forces to be in equilibrium? Try this: hang a ring between two spring balances pulled in opposite directions. When the ring is at rest, both readings are equal . Now try keeping the ring still with the two balances NOT on the same straight line — you simply can't!
The two forces must be equal in magnitude.
They must act in opposite directions.
They must act along the same straight line.

Imagine pulling a block of wood from both sides with spring balances. Equal pulls — the block stays still. Pull harder on one side, and the block moves toward the stronger pull — because the resultant is no longer zero.
A book on a table: its weight (W) pulls down; the table pushes up with a normal reaction (R). W = R, opposite, same line — so the book doesn't fall.
An object hanging from a rope: weight W down; the rope's tension (T) up. T = W — so the object stays at rest.

A bunch of bananas hangs from a light rod by three cords. All three forces are parallel — two pull up, the bananas' weight pulls down. This is a classic example of three parallel forces in equilibrium.
Another one — a child sitting on a swing. Two ropes pull up (F₁, F₂), and the child's weight (W) pulls down. These three forces balance, so the child stays at rest. Here, F₁ + F₂ = W.
All three forces must lie in one plane.
One force must act opposite to the other two.
The resultant of two of the forces must equal the third in magnitude and be opposite in direction.

You've seen a picture hung on a wall with two slanting cords. The cord tensions F₁ and F₂ are slanted (not parallel), and the picture's weight W pulls down. These three forces balance, so the picture stays still.

Hang a thin plate by a thread from three different points, and each time mark the vertical line of the thread on the plate. All three lines meet at one point — the plate's centre of gravity! This shows that for three slanting forces in equilibrium, their lines of action always meet at a single point.
All three forces must lie in one plane.
Their lines of action must meet at a single point.
The resultant of two must be equal to the third, in the opposite direction.
The same idea works for more than three forces — hang a board by four ropes at its corners and the four upward tensions together equal the board's weight, so it stays at rest.
You need all three conditions! For two forces, equal size alone isn't enough — they must also be opposite and along the same line.
Equilibrium doesn't only mean "not moving". Zero resultant means the object is either at rest or moving at a steady speed.
Unequal forces mean no equilibrium. With 20 N and 25 N opposed, there's a 5 N net force — the object moves toward the bigger pull.
For three slanting forces, the lines must meet at one point. Even if they're in one plane, no common meeting point means no equilibrium.

headings: 15.1 Pressure: force on each square metre

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you observed water pressure and hydraulic lifting. Below are the formulas (P = hρg), SI units, and exam calculations!

Press your palm flat on a table, then press the sharp tip of a pencil with the same force. The pencil tip hurts, the palm does not. The force is the same, but the tip has a much smaller area. That idea is called pressure .

The unit of pressure is newton per square metre (N m -2 ). To honour the French scientist Blaise Pascal it is called the pascal (Pa) : 1 N m -2 = 1 Pa. Pressure has only a size and no direction, so it is a scalar .

A solid presses on the table because its weight spreads over the contact area. In the same way a liquid presses on the bottom of its container, and on the vertical walls too. Let us see what this hydrostatic pressure is like.
A polythene bag with holes, filled with water: water leaves through every hole, whichever way the hole faces. So the pressure acts in every direction .
A bottle with holes at the same level near the bottom: every stream travels the same distance. So the pressure at the same level is the same.
A bottle with holes from top to bottom: the lower holes shoot the water faster. So the pressure increases with depth .

Take a column of liquid of height h and density ρ standing on a base of area 1 m². Its mass is ρ × (1 × h) = hρ, so its weight is hρg . This weight spreads over 1 m², so the pressure at the bottom is hρg. The same works at any depth inside the liquid.
A liquid cannot be squeezed into a smaller volume. So a pressure made at one point of a liquid is passed on to every other point. Machines built on this idea are called hydraulic machines .
The liquid's own weight is tiny compared with these forces, so it is ignored in the calculation.

Vehicle hoist at a service station: a small force on a small piston is transmitted through oil to a large piston carrying the vehicle. (Real hoists use a compressor to pump oil, because moving a small piston a long way is hard.)
Hydraulic jack : lifts one side of a vehicle when a wheel must be removed. A force on a small piston lifts a large piston.

Vehicle brakes : the pedal pushes the piston of the master cylinder; the oil carries the pressure to the slave cylinder at the wheel. The slave cylinder is wider, so it presses the brake pads harder than the driver pushes the pedal.
Gases press too. A gas can make pressure in two ways: by the weight of a column of gas (this is how atmospheric pressure comes about), or when a compressed gas tries to expand.
Water in a U-tube stands at the same level in both arms. Connect a balloon full of air to arm X and open it: the water in X goes down and in Y goes up.
So the compressed air in the balloon makes extra pressure on the water in X.

The atmosphere is the layer of air around the Earth, hundreds of kilometres thick. Just as water presses on a point at the bottom of a pond, the weight of the air above any point makes the atmospheric pressure .
Fill a glass tube (about 1 m long, closed at one end) with mercury.
Turn it upside down without letting air in, and stand it in a dish of mercury.
The mercury drops a little and stops with a column about 76 cm high. Above it is empty space: a vacuum.

The atmospheric pressure outside pushes on the dish and balances the 76 cm column, so the height of the column measures the atmospheric pressure. Push the tube deeper or tilt it: the vertical height stays 76 cm. Going up a mountain the air column gets shorter, so the pressure falls (about 25 cm Hg on top of Everest).

Two instruments measure atmospheric pressure: the mercury barometer above, and the aneroid barometer , which has no liquid. It has a sealed metal box with the air pumped out; when the outside pressure changes the thin walls bend, and a pointer moves over a scale.
Drinking with a straw: sucking lowers the pressure inside the straw; the atmospheric pressure on the juice outside pushes it up the straw.

Siphon: fill a tube with water, lower one end below the level of tank A. The pressure at the end in A (water column + atmosphere) is higher than the pressure at the free end, so water flows to the lower tank B.
Rubber sucker: pressed on glass, it pushes out most of the air. The pressure inside is lower than outside, so the atmosphere holds it on (only if no air leaks in at the edge).

A stone sinks but a piece of wood floats. Push a floating plank down and you feel the water pushing back up. Even a sinking object feels lighter in water than in air. The upward force that a fluid exerts on an object in it is called the upthrust .
In the activity the object that floats (partly or fully submerged) has an upthrust equal to its weight. The object that sinks has a weight greater than the upthrust.

equal to its weight → it floats fully submerged .
greater than its weight → it rises and floats partly submerged , until the upthrust equals its weight.

A hydrometer is a glass instrument with a bulb loaded with mercury or lead shot, so it floats upright. It sinks only a little in a dense liquid (little liquid has to be displaced) and more in a light liquid. The density is read straight from the scale.

headings: 18.2 Energy: the ability to do work

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you watched work and energy transfers in action. Below are the exact formulas, Joules and Watts units, and step-by-step problem solving!

You already know a force can change the position or shape of an object. When a force makes an object move, we say the force does work . Push the object with a constant 1 N until it moves 1 m along the direction of the force : the work done is defined to be one joule (1 J) .
With 2 N through 1 m the work is 2 J, with 3 N through 1 m it is 3 J. So the work depends on the force and on the distance moved.
Energy is the ability to do work. It is measured in the same unit as work, the joule (J) . We need energy for every task, and it comes in many forms.
Mechanical energy : the kind we study here, in two forms, potential energy and kinetic energy
If there is no energy loss, the work done equals the energy used up.
Both are measured in joules (J).

The energy an object has because it is moving is its kinetic energy . Send object A along the floor to hit a light trolley B: the trolley moves some distance and stops. Send A faster: the trolley goes further. Send a heavier A at the same speed: again the trolley goes further. Part of A's kinetic energy is passed to the trolley.
So the kinetic energy depends on two factors: velocity and mass .

The energy stored in an object because of its position or because its form has changed is its potential energy . When you lift an object you do work on it; that energy is stored in the object as potential energy. Let us find the energy needed to lift 3 kg through 2 m.

Work done = weight × height lifted = m g × h. The work is stored in the object, so at a height of 2 m its potential energy is 60 J. Because the work is done against gravity, it is called gravitational potential energy .
The potential energy depends on three things: the mass , the gravitational acceleration and the height . Release the object and the stored energy turns back into kinetic energy.
When a rubber band or a spring is stretched by a force, its shape changes and the work done is stored in it. This is called elastic potential energy .

A cyclist rides fast along a flat road, then reaches a hill and stops pedalling. The bicycle still climbs, but slows down: its kinetic energy decreases while its potential energy increases . At the top the kinetic energy is smallest and the potential energy is greatest. Rolling down the other side, the potential energy falls and the kinetic energy grows again.
A → B: speed falls, height rises: kinetic energy changes into potential energy.
At B the velocity is zero: all the kinetic energy has become potential energy.
B → A: the potential energy changes back into kinetic energy.
Hydro-electricity: water stored high in a reservoir falls to a lower level. Its potential energy becomes kinetic energy, which turns a turbine to make electricity.
Pile and tower: a heavy pile is lifted and released to fall on the soil, packing loose soil before a building's foundation is laid.
Sledge hammer: the lifted hammer has potential energy. Released onto a wedge, it hits with a large velocity, passes its kinetic energy to the wedge and splits the wood or stone.

The work done in a unit time, the rate of doing work , is called power . If 600 J of work is done in 10 s, the power is 600 J ÷ 10 s = 60 J s -1 . One joule per second is one watt (W) , so this power is 60 W.

headings: 19.5 What changes the resistance of a conductor?

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you observed electrons flowing in circuits. Below are Ohm's Law, circuit diagrams, and resistance calculations!

Electricity is a very important form of energy. Bulbs, irons and fans all work with it. It has two forms: static electricity , charges that sit on the surface of insulators and do not flow, and current electricity , where charges flow.
Rub a drinking straw with a piece of cotton cloth and bring it near tiny bits of paper: the bits are attracted. A straw that was not rubbed attracts nothing.
A plastic rod, pen or comb rubbed on your hair attracts tiny bits of paper or rigifoam too.

All materials are made of atoms. An atom has protons (positive), neutrons (no charge) and electrons (negative). Protons and neutrons are in the centre, the nucleus ; electrons move around it. Only electrons can be removed easily.
If rubbing removes electrons from the surface, the surface becomes positively (+) charged.
If the surface receives electrons from the cloth, it becomes negatively (−) charged.
Charges that stay still on an object are electrostatic charges . When they start to move, they make an electric current .

In Activity 19.1 a PVC rod is charged by rubbing it with polythene and touched to a neon bulb whose other terminal is earthed. The stored charges flow out through the bulb and it lights up for a moment. Charges flowing like this are an electric current .

Materials that let a current of electrons pass easily are conductors . All metals (copper, aluminium, iron) are conductors. The electrons in the outermost shell of a metal atom come loose easily and move at random between the atoms. These are the free electrons , and they are why electricity flows easily through metals.

The negative terminal of a cell repels electrons; the positive terminal attracts them. Join the two terminals with a conductor and the free electrons all start to drift from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
The electrons really flow from the negative to the positive terminal.
By convention the electric current is said to flow the opposite way: from the positive to the negative terminal.
The SI unit of current is the ampere (A) , measured with an ammeter . The ammeter must be connected so that the whole current passes through it, that is, in series .

Water runs faster from a tank placed higher, because the pressure difference between the tank and the tap is bigger. The current in a circuit is like this water flow: the source of electricity acts like the tank.

The EMF of a cell equals the potential difference across its terminals when no current is drawn . When a current is drawn it also passes through the cell, which has its own resistance, so some voltage is lost inside; subtract it from the EMF to get the potential difference given to the outside circuit.

Because it is measured in volts, the potential difference is also called the voltage . It is measured with a voltmeter , whose two terminals are connected across the two points, that is, in parallel .
Connection 1: both positive terminals go to the bulb: no potential difference, no current, bulb off.
Connection 2: both negative terminals go to the bulb: again none, bulb off.
Connection 3: one positive and one negative terminal: there is a potential difference, a current flows and the bulb lights.
So for a current to flow through a conductor, a potential difference must exist across it.

When a potential difference is put across a conductor, a current flows. In Activity 19.3 a nichrome coil is connected to two dry cells, a rheostat, an ammeter and a voltmeter. The rheostat changes the current, and you record five pairs of readings. The switch is closed only briefly, so that the coil does not heat up and the temperature stays constant.
For each reading divide V by I. If the temperature was kept constant, the ratio V/I is always the same number. This was discovered by the German scientist Georg Simon Ohm .
The unit of resistance is the ohm (Ω) : a conductor has a resistance of 1 Ω if a current of 1 A flows when 1 V is across it. Resistance is measured with an ohm meter.

The resistance of a piece of conductor depends on three things: its cross-sectional area , its length and the material it is made of. In Activity 19.4 the same cells push current through seven wires, and the ammeter readings differ because the resistances differ.
Thicker wire (bigger cross-sectional area): resistance decreases .
Longer wire: resistance increases .
Same length and area but a different metal : different currents for the same voltage, because of a property of the material called resistivity .

A tap controls the flow of water in a pipe by putting an obstacle in the way. In a circuit, raising the resistance lowers the current. Components made to give a chosen resistance are called resistors . In Activity 19.5 you connect a 5 Ω, 10 Ω or 20 Ω resistor in the torch bulb circuit: the larger the resistor, the dimmer the bulb, so the current falls as the resistance rises.
Fixed resistors: a thin film of carbon on an insulator, or a coil of a high-resistance material such as nichrome. Their value cannot be changed (for example 10 Ω, 100 Ω, 1.2 kΩ).

Variable resistors: the value can be changed by hand or with a screw: pre-adjustment resistors, rheostats, volume controls. Used in radio volume controls, to adjust circuits and to vary currents in experiments.
Light dependent resistors (LDR): made of chemicals such as cadmium sulphide. In the dark the resistance is high; in light it is low. Used in circuits that must react to the amount of light.

The value of a fixed resistor is often shown by colour bands . With four bands, the first two give the digits, the third gives the power of ten to multiply by, and the fourth (set a little apart) gives the tolerance . Gold and silver as the third band mean 10 -1 and 10 -2 .
If you cannot find a resistor of the value you need, you can join several. There are two basic ways: series and parallel .

In series the same current I flows through every resistor. The potential differences across them are V₁ = I R₁, V₂ = I R₂, V₃ = I R₃ and they add up to the supply voltage: V = I R = I R₁ + I R₂ + I R₃.
In parallel the total current divides among the resistors: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃. Each resistor has the same potential difference V across it, so V/R = V/R₁ + V/R₂ + V/R₃, which gives the rule below.

An electric shock happens when your body becomes part of a path along which electrons can flow. A complete circuit and a potential difference are both needed. With only one contact point, or two points at the same voltage, there is no danger.

People are different from birds: they usually stand on the ground. One side of a power system is deliberately connected to earth, so a person touching a single live wire connects two points of the circuit: the wire and the earth.

"It is current that kills" is largely true, but a current needs a voltage to push it. The current through the body is I = V ÷ R: the higher the voltage, the larger the current, and the larger the body's resistance, the smaller the current. Body resistance is not fixed: it changes from person to person and with how the skin touches (hand to hand, hand to foot and so on). That is why HIGH VOLTAGE signs are put up.

headings: 4.2 Describing a wave: amplitude, wavelength, period, frequency, speed

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you watched wave propagation and vibrations. Below are the official wave equations (v = fλ), diagrams, and sound calculations!

Drop a pebble on still water: a disturbance spreads out in circles. Shake one end of a rope up and down: a disturbance runs along the rope. A disturbance that travels through a medium or through space is a wave .
The ball bobs up and down, so energy reached it through the water wave, but the water particles do not travel along with the wave.
Waves can travel through a medium : water, a rope, air (sound), liquids and solids.
Some waves need no medium : light and heat from the Sun reach the Earth across empty space as electromagnetic waves . Radio waves are electromagnetic waves too.

Waves that need a material medium are mechanical waves : water waves, sound in air, and the waves on a plucked guitar string. A slinky (a steel coil) lets us study them. Shake a slinky sideways on a table, and a wave runs along it.
In a transverse wave the particles that have moved furthest up are at the crests (A, B in Figure 4.7) and those furthest down are at the troughs (C, D).

We study the simplest waves, sinusoidal waves. A particle in the wave goes from zero displacement to a maximum, back through zero, to a maximum in the other direction and back to zero. That is one oscillation (or vibration).
Amplitude: the maximum displacement of the particles taking part in the wave.
Wavelength (λ): the distance between a particle and the closest particle in the same state of motion, for example between two consecutive crests or troughs.
Period (T): the time a particle takes for one complete oscillation; also the time the wave takes to travel one wavelength.
Frequency (f): the number of oscillations a particle makes in one second. Unit: hertz (Hz) , one oscillation per second.
A wave moves one wavelength λ in one period T, so its speed is v = λ ÷ T. Because f = 1 ÷ T, this is v = f × λ.

Electromagnetic waves need no material medium. They are made of an electric field and a magnetic field that oscillate at right angles to each other, and the wave travels at right angles to both. So they are transverse waves.
They are not affected by external electric or magnetic fields.
In a vacuum they all travel at 3 × 10 8 m s -1 (more exactly 2.988 × 10 8 ).
The different frequency ranges behave differently; together they are the electromagnetic spectrum .
Visible light : 4.28 × 10 14 to 7.69 × 10 14 Hz (wavelengths 690 nm to 400 nm). Violet has the shortest wavelength; then indigo, blue, … up to red: the seven colours of the rainbow.
Gamma rays : from radioactive elements; extremely high energy; pass through steel and concrete; destroy living cells, so they treat cancer and sterilise food utensils and surgical instruments.

X rays : made by fast electrons hitting a metal target. They pass easily through soft tissue but are absorbed by bones, so they photograph the inside of the body, and are used to check baggage and cargo. Too much exposure can cause cancer.

Ultraviolet : "above violet"; bees can see it. Sunlight has a little; it makes vitamin D, but too much causes cataract and skin cancer. Used to kill germs in hospitals and to check hidden marks on banknotes.
Infrared ("heat rays"): from hot bodies, felt as warmth; heat photographs, TV remote controls, phone and computer cameras, physiotherapy.
Microwaves : radar, mobile phones and microwave ovens. Water and fat in food absorb them and heat up; a magnetron makes them.
Radio waves : the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies; long-distance communication. Information is added by changing the amplitude or the frequency of the wave; antennas send and receive them.
All sounds are made by vibrating objects : a bee's wings, a cricket rubbing its wings, our vocal cords. The type of energy that gives the sensation of hearing is acoustic energy .

A loud-speaker membrane moves to the right and pushes air molecules together: a compression . It moves left and leaves a rarefaction . These compressions and rarefactions travel forward at the same speed; each air molecule only moves back and forth about its place. So sound is a longitudinal wave.

Ring an electric bell inside a bell jar and pump the air out: the sound gets fainter and finally disappears. So sound cannot travel through a vacuum: it is a mechanical wave and needs a medium (unlike light).

Sound goes faster in warmer air, faster in water than in air (about four times), and fastest in solids. Light is far quicker (3 × 10 8 m s -1 ), which is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.
Three characteristics of sound let us tell sounds apart: pitch , loudness and quality . Each is a sensation in the ear linked to a property of the wave.
Pitch depends on the frequency . Clamp a hacksaw blade and twang it: lengthen the free end and the frequency and pitch fall. Middle C is 256 Hz and higher C is 512 Hz, twice the pitch.
Loudness depends on the energy the wave carries to the ear, which depends on the amplitude . Pluck a string harder: more work, larger amplitude, louder sound.
Quality depends on the shape of the waveform . A tuning fork, a violin and a piano playing the same note with the same loudness still sound different, because their waveforms differ.
A regular repeating waveform sounds pleasant (music). An irregular waveform with no repeating pattern is noise .

The human ear hears frequencies from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz : the hearing range . Below 20 Hz is infrasound ; above 20 000 Hz is ultrasound . The upper limit falls with age. Elephants hear infrasound; dogs hear up to about 40 000 Hz; rabbits, dolphins and bats hear ultrasound.
Bats send out ultrasound and judge the position of obstacles from the echo. Dolphins use it to find small fish, to avoid sharks and to talk to each other.
SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging): a ship sends an ultrasound pulse down; the depth comes from the time the echo takes to return: distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
Medical scans : the heart (size, pulse, blood pumped), the womb and the baby; lithotripsy breaks bladder stones.
Flaw detection : ultrasound in a solid does not pass an air gap, so cracks in aircraft parts show up. Also spectacles for blind people and soldering metals.
A musical instrument is built to make periodic vibrations , a repeating waveform. There are three main types.

In Sector 1, you observed light rays bending and reflecting. Below are the ray diagrams, focal length rules, and refractive index calculations!

We see an object only if light from it reaches our eyes. Luminous objects (a candle flame, a bulb) give out their own light. Non-luminous objects only reflect light that falls on them. Materials can be transparent (glass), translucent (tissue paper: light passes but you cannot see clearly) or opaque (stone).
It is virtual : no light actually passes through it, so it cannot be caught on a screen.
Image distance = object distance (as far behind the mirror as the object is in front).
Same size and upright, but laterally inverted : left and right swap. That is why AMBULANCE is printed reversed on the front of the van.

A mirror with a curved reflecting surface is a curved mirror ; if the surface is part of a sphere, a spherical mirror . A concave mirror curves inward (dentists' and shaving mirrors give enlarged images). A convex mirror curves outward (vehicle side mirrors and shop security mirrors show a wide view as small images).
Centre of curvature (C): the centre of the sphere the mirror is part of.
Pole (P): the centre point of the mirror surface.
Principal axis: the line through P and C, perpendicular to the mirror at P.
Focal point (F): the point where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to come from (convex). It lies halfway between P and C.
Focal length (f) = distance PF; radius of curvature r = distance PC = 2 f.
A ray along the principal axis comes straight back.
A ray parallel to the axis is reflected through F . A ray through F is reflected parallel to the axis.
A ray through C is reflected back along its own path (the radius is a normal to the surface).
To find the image of a vertical object on the axis, draw two of these rays from the top of the object; the image of the top is where they meet. The foot of the image stays on the axis.

A convex mirror reflects parallel rays as a divergent beam that seems to come from F behind the mirror. Whatever the distance of the object, the image is upright, virtual and smaller , and you cannot catch it on a screen.

A pencil in a glass of water looks bent, and a coin at the bottom looks raised. Light bends when it goes from one medium into another with different optical properties. This bending is refraction . The rays from the coin bend away from the normal as they leave the water, so they seem to come from a point higher up: the apparent depth is less than the real depth.

The cause is the change in the speed of light . Light travels at 3 × 10 8 m s -1 in a vacuum and slower in other media. A medium where light is slower is denser (optically); where it is faster, rarer . A ray bends only if it meets the boundary at an angle other than 90°.

In the glass block: AB is the incident ray , BC the refracted ray (bent towards the normal on entering glass), CD the emergent ray (bent away on leaving). The angles with the normal are the angle of incidence i, of refraction r and of emergence e.
If the first medium is a vacuum, n depends on the second medium only; since light in air is almost as fast as in a vacuum, the n of a medium relative to air is used as the n of that medium.

When light goes from a dense to a rare medium it bends away from the normal. Increase the angle of incidence inside the dense medium: at one angle, the critical angle c , the refracted ray runs along the boundary (angle of refraction 90°). For any larger angle all the light is reflected back into the dense medium: total internal reflection .

Optical fibres: thin flexible glass or plastic fibres. Light entering one end travels along by total internal reflection and leaves at the far end with almost no loss, even over many kilometres. Used in the endoscope (to see inside the body), telephone and Internet links, and decorations.

Prisms: a prism with angles 90°, 45°, 45° turns a ray through 90°. The ray enters the first face straight, hits the second face at 45° (more than the critical angle of glass) and is totally reflected, leaving the third face straight. Used in cameras, telescopes and binoculars.

A lens is a curved piece of transparent material (glass, plastic, even water) that bends light by refraction. Lenses are in spectacles, cameras, binoculars, telescopes, microscopes, magnifying glasses, and in our eyes. Types: bi-convex and plano-convex (convex lenses), bi-concave and plano-concave (concave lenses).
Principal axis: the line through the two centres of curvature. A ray along it passes through undeviated.
Optical centre (C): the middle of the lens. A ray through it passes straight, undeviated.

Focal point (F): a convex lens bends parallel rays so that they meet at F; it has one F on each side at the same distance, the focal length f . A concave lens spreads parallel rays so that they seem to come from F.
A ray through the optical centre goes straight on.
A ray parallel to the axis passes through F after the lens.
A ray through F comes out parallel to the axis.

A concave lens never forms a real image. You see an upright, diminished, virtual image whatever the object distance. (The printed chapter summary says "convex" in two places, but its own sections 5.4.1 and 5.4.2 show it is the concave lens that always gives this.)
Hand lens (simple microscope): a convex lens with a handle. With the object closer than f, it gives a magnified, upright, virtual image: for looking at insects and flower parts.
Principle of reversibility of light: if a ray is reversed it follows exactly the same path backwards, even after many reflections and refractions.

Camera: a convex lens makes a real, inverted image on the film; moving the lens changes the lens-to-film distance so that objects at different distances are sharp. The compound microscope has an objective and an eyepiece lens for a very high magnification.

headings: Watch it happen: heat, latent heat and the three ways heat travels

paragraphs.text: Heat vs Temperature: Temperature is degree of hotness; heat is thermal energy transferred between bodies.
Heat Transfer: Conduction occurs in solids without bulk motion; Convection occurs in fluids via density currents; Radiation travels via EM waves through vacuum.
Specific Heat Capacity: Heat energy required to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C: Q = m × c × Δθ.

headings: 9.3 Heat capacity and specific heat capacity
9.4 Change of state and latent heat

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you saw heat expanding and transferring. Below are the thermal formulas (Q = mcΔθ), Joules per kilogram units, and calorimetry calculations!

Temperature tells how hot or cold an object is. It is a measure of the mean kinetic energy of the particles of the object. Touch is not accurate and gives no number, so we use a thermometer (the first was made by Galileo Galilei around 1600 A.D.).

Glass-mercury thermometer: mercury in a bulb expands up a narrow tube; the scale is read from the length of the column. Mercury expands uniformly, conducts heat well and is liquid from −39 °C to 357 °C, but it is toxic, so these are used less now.
Glass-alcohol thermometer: ethanol (coloured) instead of mercury. It melts at −115 °C, so it suits very low temperatures, and expands a lot and uniformly.
Digital thermometer: uses an electrical property, such as resistance, that depends on temperature.
Celsius scale: the melting point of pure ice is 0 °C and the boiling point of water is 100 °C (at one atmosphere); these fixed points are divided into 100 divisions.
Fahrenheit scale: ice melts at 32 °F and water boils at 212 °F: 180 divisions.

Kelvin scale: Lord Kelvin showed there is a lowest possible temperature, absolute zero (−273.15 °C), when the particles have no kinetic energy. 0 K is absolute zero, and 1 K is the same size as 1 °C. The Kelvin is the international unit of temperature.

Light a burner under one of two identical vessels of water: its temperature rises, the other stays the same. Something has moved from the flame to the water: heat . Heat is the energy transferred from one object to another because of a temperature difference. It is a form of energy (Count Rumford showed this in 1798; James Joule investigated it from 1840), measured in joules (J) ; the calorie is also used.
Heat flows from the body at the higher temperature to the body at the lower temperature, like water flowing downhill.
The cooler body warms up; the hotter body cools down.
When both reach the same temperature, there is no more flow: thermal equilibrium .

Heat equal amounts to water and to coconut oil, or to one beaker of water and a beaker with double the water (Activity 9.2): the temperature rises differ. Different objects need different amounts of heat for the same rise.
Heat capacity (C): the heat needed to raise the temperature of an object by one unit. Unit: J K -1 (or J °C -1 ). It depends on the substance and the mass.
Specific heat capacity (c): the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by one degree. Unit: J kg -1 K -1 . It depends only on the substance.

A substance can be a solid, liquid or gas, and heating or cooling changes its state: melting, freezing (solidifying), boiling and condensing are changes of state . The melting point is the temperature at which a heated solid becomes liquid; the freezing point of a substance has the same value. The boiling point is where a liquid forms bubbles inside and becomes vapour. All of them depend on the pressure (usually quoted at 1 atmosphere).

Heat ice that is just below 0 °C: its temperature rises to 0 °C. Then, while it melts, the temperature does not rise even though heat is still supplied. The heat is spent working against the attractive forces between the molecules. This hidden heat, absorbed with no temperature change during a change of state, is the latent heat . Once all the ice has become water at 0 °C, extra heat raises the temperature again. When the water reaches 100 °C the same happens again as it turns to steam.
Latent heat of fusion: the heat absorbed when ice at 0 °C becomes water at 0 °C. The same amount is released when water freezes.
Specific latent heat of fusion of ice: 3.36 × 10 5 J kg -1 : the heat to change 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C.
Specific latent heat of vaporization of water: 2.26 × 10 6 J kg -1 : the heat to change 1 kg of water at 100 °C into steam at 100 °C. Steam gives the same heat out when it condenses.

Vaporization is turning into gas. It happens by boiling (at the boiling point, with bubbles inside the liquid) or by evaporation (slowly, only at the surface, at any temperature below the boiling point). Both absorb latent heat. Evaporation dries clothes, and sweating cools us: the large latent heat of water takes a lot of heat from the skin.

The increase in length, area or volume of a substance when it is heated is thermal expansion ; the decrease on cooling is contraction . Two stuck glasses can be parted by pouring cold water in the inner one and standing the outer one in warm water. An iron ball that just passes through a ring will no longer pass when hot (Activity 9.3).

Solids: iron rims are fitted to wooden cart wheels while hot; railway rails have small gaps; telephone and power cables hang loosely between poles; a tight metal bottle lid opens after being warmed (metal expands more than glass).
Liquids: the liquid in mercury and alcohol thermometers expands up the tube (in Activity 9.4 the level first drops as the glass expands, then rises as the liquid expands more).
Gases: warm the air in a bottle and the balloon on its mouth inflates; it shrinks again when the air cools (Activity 9.5).

A bimetallic strip has two metals that expand by different amounts riveted together. When heated it bends, so it can switch off an electric heater when the temperature gets too high. It is used in electric irons and rice cookers to control the temperature.
Heat is really the random kinetic energy of particles (vibration, rotation, translation). Heat transfer is the spreading of that energy from a hotter region to a colder region, in three ways.
Good conductors: silver, copper, iron, mercury, aluminium. Insulators: wood, plastic, asbestos, clay, wool, air. Water is a very poor conductor.
A robin fluffs its feathers to trap air, a poor conductor, so it stays warm. Seals have a thick layer of fat (blubber) to stop heat loss.
An immersion heater must be fully immersed or placed low: if only the top is heated, the water near the top gets hot and the bottom stays cool, because convection currents do not flow downwards.
Sea breeze (day): land has a smaller specific heat capacity than sea water, so it heats up faster; the air above it warms, rises and lowers the pressure, and cool air flows from the sea to the land.
Land breeze (night): the land cools quickly and the sea slowly, so the air over the sea is warmer and rises; wind blows from the land to the sea.
Dark and rough surfaces absorb radiation well. Shiny, polished and white surfaces reflect it well.

Cricketers wear white in the sun; people in cold climates wear dark colours indoors; black cooking pots absorb heat fast; the inside of a thermos flask is silvered to reflect heat back or keep it out.

headings: Watch it happen: power, energy and the house circuit

paragraphs.text: Electrical Power: Power consumed by an appliance: P = V × I = I²R = V² / R (Watts).
Electrical Energy (Units): Energy = Power (kW) × Time (hours) = kWh (Electricity Units).
Electrical Safety: Fuses and circuit breakers protect against overload; earth wire directs leak currents safely into the ground.

headings: 10.1 Power of an appliance: P = V I
10.2 Electric energy used: E = P t

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you saw home appliances consuming power. Below are the power formulas (P = VI), kWh unit calculations, and safety rules!

We use electric energy by converting it into the form we need. An electric appliance is a device that does this: an electric heater, oven and induction cooker give heat ; a motor gives kinetic energy ; a fluorescent lamp gives light ; a radio gives sound ; a television gives light and sound.

In some appliances there is a second conversion: a filament bulb first turns electric energy into heat, and the hot filament then gives light; a fluorescent lamp makes ultraviolet radiation first, which is then turned into visible light.

Power is the energy used in a unit time. For an appliance working with a voltage V and drawing a current I, the power is the product of the two. With V in volts and I in amperes, P comes out in watts (W) .

In the heating coil of an oven all the electric energy becomes heat. In some other appliances part of the energy becomes heat because of the internal resistance, and the rest changes into the useful form (light, motion, sound).
The energy used by an appliance depends on how long it works. If it uses P in each second, the energy used in a time t is P t.
The same job can be done by different appliances. A more efficient one wastes less energy as heat. If 40 % of the energy supplied is lost as heat, only 60 % is useful: the efficiency is 60 %.
LED bulbs are the best (lowest power, longest life), but their higher first cost limits their use in Sri Lanka.

Cooking and heating: old coil cookers are least efficient. An immersion heater is very efficient for water (all its heat goes into the water). Hot-plate rice cookers lose less heat. Microwave ovens heat inside the food. Induction cookers use a changing magnetic field to heat only the bottom of the pan.
LCD (LED) televisions use less power than old cathode ray tube TVs; table fans are more efficient than ceiling fans for cooling a room.
Iron all the week's clothes at once, switch off unwanted lights and use CFL or LED bulbs.

Power stations raise the voltage to 132 kV or 220 kV with step-up transformers for the national grid; sub-stations lower it to 33 kV or 11 kV and finally to 230 V , an alternating current of 50 Hz , for houses. The service cable has two wires, the live wire and the neutral wire.

Overload circuit breaker (older houses: service fuse ): about 40 A, on the live wire only. If a larger current passes, it disconnects the house. The fuse wire (lead and tin alloy) melts. It belongs to the electricity provider.
Electricity meter: counts the energy in kilowatt hours (kW h) for billing. It also belongs to the provider.
Isolator (older: main switch with a 30 A fuse): a dual-pole switch that disconnects both live and neutral wires, used for repairs. Everything after the isolator belongs to the consumer.

RCCB (trip switch): protects people from electric shock. It cuts the supply automatically when current leaks to the metal casing of an appliance or to earth (about 35 mA), or when more than 30 A flows. It works by electromagnetic induction. Press its test button every few days. It is switched on by raising the lever.

Distribution box: sends electricity to lighting circuits (6 A MCB: bulbs and 6 A plugs) and plug circuits (13 A MCB: kitchen heaters, ovens). An MCB (older: fuses of 5 A and 15 A) trips when the circuit current is too large, so only that circuit goes off. MCBs and fuses protect against short circuits and overheated cables only, not against shock. They are always connected on the live wire.
One of the two supply wires is earthed near the transformer: this neutral wire is at about 0 V. The other wire is at 230 V compared with the earth.
A person on the ground touching the live wire has 230 V across the body: 50 mA is a major shock and 100 mA can kill. That is why it is called the "live" wire.
This is needed for the RCCB to work: if the live wire touches earth anywhere in the house, the RCCB detects the large current and cuts the supply.

Switches turn bulbs on and off one at a time. Plug sockets have live, neutral and earth connections; the larger pin of a three-pin plug is connected to the metal body of the appliance and, through the socket, to the earth wire, so a leak trips the RCCB. Appliances with an insulating plastic cover can use two-pin plugs (no earth).
Wires: copper. 1 mm² single cable for 5 to 6 A; seven-strand 1.5 mm² cable for 13 or 15 A plug circuits. Colours: brown live, blue neutral, green earth (older: red live, black neutral).

Each bulb and plug is connected in parallel . All switches are on the live wire, so touching a bulb holder with the switch off gives no shock. Plug circuits are sometimes ring circuits : each socket gets current through two wires, so thinner cable can be used.
Turn the overload circuit breaker OFF first, then raise the lever of the RCCB or MCB that tripped, then turn the overload breaker ON. If it trips again, call an electrician.
Use only 6 A and 13 A fuses. Do not overload a socket with many appliances through a multi-plug. Put only proper plugs into a socket, never bare wires.
Wear rubber slippers or stand on a rubber mat when ironing; use a mat in front of a fridge.
Switch off the overload circuit breaker or main switch before changing a bulb in a bathroom. Unplug appliances when not in use.
In strong lightning unplug radios and TVs and avoid unnecessary appliances (the RCCB does not protect against lightning).

Never use electrical devices with a wet body or touch switches with wet hands. Do not switch on appliances during a power cut. In a fire, switch off the overload circuit breaker. Repairs and extensions only by a trained electrician.
The joule is small, so electricity bills use the kilowatt hour (kW h) , also called a unit : the energy used in one hour by an appliance of power 1 kW. The meter counts it.

headings: 11.3 The p-n junction and the diode

paragraphs.text: In Sector 1, you observed electronic gates and diodes in action. Below are the semiconductor circuit diagrams, biasing rules, and transistor functions!

Electronic devices such as phones, computers, televisions and radios are built from special materials. Conductors (copper, aluminium, iron, lead; alloys such as brass, nichrome, manganin) have electrons in the outer shell that are loosely held and move freely. Insulators (ebonite, polythene, plastic, dry wood, asbestos, glass) have strong bonds, so almost no electrons are free. Semiconductors conduct a little.

Silicon (Si) and germanium (Ge), in crystal form, are semiconductors. They are in group IV and have four outer electrons. Each atom shares them with four neighbours in covalent bonds , giving eight outer electrons: a stable crystal lattice.

These bonds are weak: even at room temperature the thermal energy breaks some, freeing electrons. Each freed electron leaves a hole , a missing electron that acts like a positive charge . An electron from a neighbouring atom can jump into the hole, so the hole moves too. In a semiconductor both electrons (negative carriers) and holes (positive carriers) carry current; their numbers are equal, so the crystal stays neutral. In a metal only electrons carry the current.
Conductors: higher temperature means more random motion of the free electrons, which obstructs the current: conductivity decreases (resistivity increases).
Semiconductors: higher temperature breaks more bonds, giving more holes and electrons: conductivity increases (resistivity decreases).
Pure silicon or germanium is an intrinsic semiconductor. Adding ( doping ) a tiny amount of another element makes an extrinsic semiconductor with many more carriers.

Dope one half of a crystal p-type and the other half n-type: where they meet is a p-n junction . Electrons from the n side diffuse across and holes from the p side diffuse the other way. They recombine and leave a region with no free carriers: the depletion layer . The p side of it gains a negative charge and the n side a positive charge, which makes a voltage that opposes further diffusion: the potential barrier (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium).
Biasing is connecting an external voltage across the junction.

Forward bias: p side to the positive terminal and n side to the negative terminal. The depletion layer narrows. When the applied voltage is above the barrier (greater than 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge) a large current flows.
Reverse bias: p side to the negative terminal and n side to the positive terminal. The depletion layer widens and no current flows.

A device made of one p-n junction is a junction diode . The p terminal is the anode (A) , the n terminal is the cathode (K) . A current flows only when the anode is connected to the positive terminal. On a real diode the white or silver ring marks the cathode. In Activity 11.1 a 2.5 V bulb with an IN4001 diode lights only when the diode is forward biased.

An alternating current (AC) keeps reversing; a direct current (DC) flows one way. Dynamos give AC, but many electronic devices need DC. A diode lets current pass one way only, so it can convert AC into DC: rectification .

Half wave rectification: a step-down transformer lowers 230 V AC to a small voltage. The single diode conducts only in the positive half cycle (X positive), so there is a current through R only half of the time.

Full wave rectification uses four diodes in a bridge . When X is positive, D1 and D4 conduct; when Y is positive, D2 and D3 conduct. In both half cycles the current flows through the load in the same direction .
The current passes through two diodes, each dropping about 0.7 V: 2 × 0.7 = 1.4 V.
Voltage left for the bulb: 4.5 − 1.4 = 3.1 V. A 3 V battery would leave only 1.6 V, not enough to light it.

Smoothing: the rectified output rises and falls between zero and a maximum, but most devices want a steady voltage like a battery gives. A large capacitor (for example 1000 μF or 2000 μF) connected in parallel with the output charges while the voltage rises and discharges when it falls, so the output hardly drops to zero. A bigger capacitance smooths better, and full wave output is smoother than half wave.
Protection: a rectifier diode in series with a DC appliance protects it if the battery is connected the wrong way round: the diode is then reverse biased and no current flows.

When a p-n junction made of a material such as gallium arsenide (GaAs) is forward biased, it gives out light : a light emitting diode (LED) . The longer terminal is the anode; the terminal next to the cut on the base is the cathode. LEDs come in red, yellow, green, blue, infrared and ultraviolet, and each colour needs a minimum forward voltage (red about 1.8 V, green 2.2 V, blue 5 V in the textbook table) with a current of 10 to 20 mA. That is why one 1.5 V dry cell cannot light an LED but two cells (3 V) can.
LEDs are used as indicators, in large TV screens, torches and street and home lighting. They use very little power and last about 50 000 hours. A brighter LED (more current) has a shorter life.

Solar cells are also p-n junctions built so that light falls on the junction. Sunlight on a silicon p-n junction produces a small EMF. Cells joined in series and parallel make a solar panel (for example 12 V to 15 V with a large current). Solar panels were first made for satellites and are now cheap enough to power homes (connected to the mains), clocks, calculators and solar cars. They use free sunlight, give out no harmful substance and last long.

A transistor has two p-n junctions: three semiconductor regions joined as npn or pnp . The three terminals are the emitter (E) and collector (C) at the two ends and the base (B) in the middle. Carriers flow from the emitter to the collector, and the base controls this flow. The arrow head in the symbol marks the emitter and shows the current direction.

In an npn transistor the carriers are electrons and the current flows from the collector to the emitter (arrow out). In a pnp transistor the carriers are holes and the current flows from the emitter to the collector (arrow in). Only npn transistors are used in this course.

Biasing: the emitter-base junction is forward biased (about 0.7 V) and the base-collector junction reverse biased with a higher voltage. For an npn transistor C goes to the positive side and E to the negative side, and B gets a smaller positive voltage than C.
A current flows in the output (collector) circuit only when a current flows in the input (base) circuit.
A small base current I B controls a large collector current I C : the small current is amplified .

The transistor also amplifies signals . In Activity 11.4 a small audio signal is fed to the base through a 0.1 μF capacitor (which passes only the changing signal), the base gets its 0.7 V forward bias through a 22 kΩ resistor, and a louder copy of the sound comes from the 8 Ω speaker in the collector circuit.
When the base-emitter voltage is below 0.7 V there is no collector current: the switch is off .
From about 0.7 V the collector current starts, and at about 0.8 V it is at its maximum: the switch is on .

The base voltage can be set with a potential divider : two resistors R1 and R2 in series across 3 V carry the same current I = 3 ÷ (R1 + R2), so V B = R2 × 3 ÷ (R1 + R2). Changing R2 changes V B between 0 and 3 V. For example, with R1 = 10 kΩ, V B = 0.7 V needs R2 = 3043 Ω.

A light dependent resistor (LDR) has a very low resistance in light (about 1 Ω) and a very high one in the dark (about 100 kΩ). With the LDR as R2 and a variable resistor as R1, darkness raises R2, so V B rises past 0.7 V and the transistor switches the bulb on; light makes the bulb go out.
